name: Rates of reaction and collision theory

questions.q: What term defines the speed at which reactants are used up or products are formed in a chemical reaction?
a: Rate of reaction
Activation energy
Enthalpy change
Equilibrium constant

questions.q: According to collision theory, what two main conditions must be met for a collision between reactant particles to be successful?
a: Low temperature and slow speed
Sufficient activation energy and correct collision geometry
High pressure and neutral pH
Equal mass and identical volume

questions.q: How does increasing the temperature of a reaction mixture affect the rate of reaction?
a: Decreases the rate because particles move slower
Has no effect on the rate
Increases the rate because particles gain kinetic energy and collide more frequently and with greater energy
Increases the rate only by changing the activation energy barrier

questions.q: Why does increasing the concentration of reactants in aqueous solution increase the rate of reaction?
a: It lowers the temperature of the mixture
It reduces the activation energy required
It increases the volume of the container
It increases the number of particles per unit volume, leading to a higher frequency of successful collisions

questions.q: How does crushing a solid reactant into a fine powder affect the rate of a chemical reaction?
a: Increases the rate by increasing the surface area exposed for collisions
Decreases the rate because smaller particles repel each other
Has no effect on the rate of reaction
Increases the rate by lowering the temperature

questions.q: What is the role of a catalyst in a chemical reaction?
a: It is permanently consumed to form products
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, increasing the rate without being used up
It increases the overall enthalpy change of the reaction
It stops unwanted side reactions completely

questions.q: Which of the following experimental methods is most suitable for measuring the rate of a reaction that produces a gas?
a: Measuring the change in pH using universal indicator
Weighing the total mass of the reactants before mixing
Collecting the gas in a gas syringe or measuring mass loss over time using a balance
Freezing the mixture and measuring solid density

questions.q: In the reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid, which change would decrease the rate of reaction?
a: Using powdered calcium carbonate instead of large lumps
Increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid
Raising the temperature of the acid solution
Diluting the hydrochloric acid with water

questions.q: What happens to the rate of a reaction as the reaction proceeds from start to finish?
a: The rate decreases over time as reactant particles are used up and their concentration falls
The rate increases constantly until an explosion occurs
The rate remains completely constant throughout
The rate drops to zero immediately and then rises

questions.q: Why does increasing gas pressure increase the rate of a gaseous reaction?
a: It increases the mass of individual molecules
It pushes gas molecules closer together, increasing the frequency of collisions
It cools the gas down
It removes activation energy barriers

questions.q: Which term describes the minimum energy that colliding particles must possess to react?
a: Lattice energy
Bond dissociation energy
Activation energy
Ionization energy

questions.q: In an experiment measuring the reaction between magnesium ribbon and dilute hydrochloric acid, hydrogen gas is evolved. What units are typically used to express the rate of this reaction?
a: g/mol
cm<sup>3</sup>
J/g
cm<sup>3</sup>/s

questions.q: What effect does a catalyst have on the position of chemical equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
a: It speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it has no effect on the equilibrium position
It shifts the equilibrium completely to the products
It shifts the equilibrium completely to the reactants
It stops the reverse reaction entirely

questions.q: Which of the following factors does not affect the rate of a chemical reaction involving solids and liquids?
a: Temperature
Pressure of the system
Concentration of the solution
Surface area of the solid

questions.q: How does a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve help explain the effect of temperature on reaction rate?
a: It shows that low-energy particles disappear
It proves that volume changes with pressure
It shows that a higher proportion of particles possess energy equal to or greater than the activation energy at higher temperatures
It demonstrates that catalysts change molecular mass

questions.q: When sodium thiosulfate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, a yellow precipitate of sulfur is formed, making the mixture cloudy. Which method is typically used to monitor this reaction rate?
a: Measuring gas volume with a gas syringe
Recording temperature changes with a data logger
Weighing mass loss on a digital balance
Timing how long it takes for a cross placed under the reaction flask to disappear from view

questions.q: Why does a lump of coal dust burn much faster and more violently than a single large lump of coal in air?
a: Coal dust has a much larger surface area to volume ratio, exposing more particles to oxygen simultaneously
Coal dust contains a higher percentage of pure carbon
Coal dust absorbs moisture from the air
Coal dust lowers the activation energy of combustion

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus is best used to measure 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrochloric acid accurately during a rate titration experiment?
a: Beaker
Pipette
Conical flask
Test tube

questions.q: In a catalyzed reaction, what happens to the catalyst after the reaction is complete?
a: It is completely destroyed
It is converted into a gas
It can be recovered chemically unchanged and retains its mass
It turns into a different element

questions.q: How does adding a catalyst affect the activation energy of a reaction?
a: Increases activation energy significantly
Doubles activation energy
Has no effect on activation energy
Lowers activation energy by providing an alternative reaction route

questions.q: Which of the following describes the effect of lowering the temperature on a reaction?
a: Decreases the rate because particles have less kinetic energy and collide less frequently with fewer successful impacts
Increases the rate due to higher density
Stops all particle motion instantly
Has no effect on particle collisions

questions.q: What is measured on the y-axis when plotting a graph of volume of gas collected against time for a fast reaction?
a: Time elapsed in seconds
Total volume of gas produced in cm<sup>3</sup>
Temperature in degrees Celsius
Mass of the flask in grams

questions.q: Why does the gradient of a gas volume versus time curve become less steep (flatten out) as time progresses?
a: The reaction speeds up as products accumulate
The temperature of the room increases
Reactants are being used up, so their concentration decreases and the reaction rate slows down
The gas syringe becomes blocked

questions.q: Which term describes a reaction that takes place so rapidly that it releases a huge amount of energy in a confined space almost instantly?
a: Slow weathering
Rusting of iron
Photosynthesis
Explosion

questions.q: If it takes 40 seconds for 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen gas to be produced in a reaction, what is the average rate of gas production during this interval?
a: 1.25 cm<sup>3</sup>/s
0.80 cm<sup>3</sup>/s
90.0 cm<sup>3</sup>/s
2.00 cm<sup>3</sup>/s

questions.q: Which factor explains why biological catalysts (enzymes) work best at a specific optimum temperature?
a: Higher temperatures destroy their shape (denature them), while low temperatures give particles insufficient kinetic energy
Enzymes freeze solid at room temperature
Enzymes turn into acids at high temperatures
Enzymes only function in a vacuum

questions.q: What is the effect of increasing the surface area of a solid reactant on the frequency of collisions?
a: Collisions become less frequent
Collisions stop entirely
Collisions occur more frequently because more surface particles are exposed
Collisions have lower energy

questions.q: In the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide using manganese(IV) oxide, what role does the manganese(IV) oxide play?
a: Reactant
Inert impurity
Product
Catalyst

questions.q: Why does a glowing relight more brightly in pure oxygen than in air?
a: Higher concentration of oxygen molecules increases collision frequency and combustion rate
Air contains poisonous gases that slow down burning
Oxygen gas is much colder than air
Nitrogen in air acts as a catalyst

questions.q: Which of the following statements about collision theory is correct?
a: Every collision between reactant particles results in a reaction
Only a small fraction of total collisions are successful because most lack the necessary activation energy or geometry
Collisions only occur when liquids are boiling
Particle speed has no impact on collision success

questions.q: How does dilution of an acid affect the rate of its reaction with a reactive metal?
a: Rate increases because water speeds up metal atoms
Rate remains completely unchanged
Rate decreases because there are fewer acid particles per unit volume, reducing collision frequency
Rate becomes infinite

questions.q: When drawing a tangent to a curve on a graph of mass loss against time, what does the gradient of that tangent represent?
a: Total mass lost
Activation energy
Final temperature
Rate of reaction at that specific instant (instantaneous rate)

questions.q: Which condition would give the fastest initial rate of reaction between marble chips (calcium carbonate) and excess dilute hydrochloric acid?
a: Fine calcium carbonate powder and 2.0 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> hydrochloric acid at 50 degrees Celsius
Large marble lumps and 0.5 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> hydrochloric acid at 20 degrees Celsius
Medium marble chips and 1.0 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> hydrochloric acid at 25 degrees Celsius
Large marble lumps and 2.0 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> hydrochloric acid at 20 degrees Celsius

questions.q: What happens to the total mass of an open reaction flask where hydrogen gas is escaping during a reaction?
a: Mass increases steadily
Mass decreases as gas escapes into the room
Mass remains constant throughout
Mass drops to zero immediately

questions.q: Why does the rate of reaction eventually drop to zero in a closed container?
a: The container walls become too hot
Products start escaping into the atmosphere
One or more reactants have been completely used up
Catalysts evaporate

questions.q: Which of the following describes an enzyme?
a: A synthetic plastic catalyst used in industry
An inorganic metal oxide powder
A radioactive isotope
A protein molecule produced by living organisms that acts as a biological catalyst

questions.q: How does an increase in gas volume at constant temperature affect pressure and reaction rate?
a: Increasing container volume decreases pressure, spreading particles out and decreasing collision rate
Increasing volume increases pressure and speeds up reactions
Volume has no effect on gas reactions
Pressure rises when volume increases

questions.q: In industrial processes, why are catalysts used even though they can be expensive?
a: They increase the theoretical maximum yield of products
They allow reactions to run at lower temperatures and pressures, saving massive energy costs
They eliminate the need for any chemical reactors
They turn waste products into pure gold

questions.q: Which of the following sets of conditions will produce sulfur dioxide gas most rapidly when reacting excess sodium sulfite with dilute hydrochloric acid?
a: Large crystals of sodium sulfite at 15 degrees Celsius
Sodium sulfite solution diluted with excess water
Concentrated hydrochloric acid and finely powdered sodium sulfite at 40 degrees Celsius
Frozen sodium sulfite blocks

questions.q: What is the primary reason food spoils more slowly when stored in a refrigerator?
a: Refrigerators introduce carbon dioxide gas
Refrigerators remove all moisture
Refrigerators block light
Lower temperatures reduce the kinetic energy and collision frequency of spoilage bacteria and chemical reactions
